clue.text: One of Cornelia's precious children

parts.note: Cornelia, mother of the Roman reformers the Gracchi, showed off her sons as her treasures in place of finery

explanation.surface: A remark about one child of a Roman matron whom she held dear.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman matron Cornelia, asked to display her ornaments, pointed to her sons and said these were hers, so each child is one of her gems.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornelia called her sons her treasures, so each is a precious gem in her own words.

clue.text: Gastronomically he had a lean time

definitions.text: Gastronomically he had a lean time

parts.words: Gastronomically he had a lean time
parts.note: the nursery-rhyme man who could eat no fat literally had only lean meat

explanation.surface: Someone who went hungry, food-wise.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme this man 'could eat no fat', so his meals were only lean.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme character ate nothing but lean meat while his wife ate the fat.

clue.text: He gained an Oscar at an early age

definitions.text: He gained an Oscar at an early age

parts.words: He gained an Oscar at an early age
parts.note: an Oscar sounds like a film award, but this man was given the first name Oscar as a baby

explanation.surface: A young actor wins an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gained an Oscar' suggests a film award; the Irish writer was simply christened Oscar.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish playwright was named Oscar at his christening, as an infant.

clue.text: Blow it, that's the end ! said the bridge-player forgetting it

definitions.text: Blow it, that's the end ! said the bridge-player forgetting it

parts.words: Blow it, that's the end ! said the bridge-player forgetting it
parts.note: the blast that ends the world in the Bible shares its name with the final top card in bridge, which a careless player may forget

explanation.surface: A card player curses after losing track of the final top card.
explanation.walkthrough: The trumpet sounded on Judgement Day is 'blown' at the end of the world; in bridge the same words mean the final remaining trump, which a forgetful player loses track of.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the trumpet call of Judgement Day and, at the card table, the final remaining trump.

clue.text: Once the main entertainment in former days

definitions.text: Once the main entertainment in former days

parts.words: Once the main entertainment in former days
parts.note: a 'main' is an old word for a match of fighting birds, so the main entertainment was a bout between gamecocks

explanation.surface: A nostalgic look back at what used to be the chief amusement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' looks like 'chief', but it is the old sporting term for a series of bouts between gamecocks.
explanation.definitionFit: A main was a contest of gamecocks, a popular spectacle before the sport was banned.

clue.text: Sound frabjously joyful

parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's poem 'Jabberwocky' the father cries 'O frabjous day!' and laughs gleefully in his joy

explanation.surface: Be heard sounding wonderfully happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frabjous' and the answer are both words coined by Lewis Carroll in 'Jabberwocky': 'O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay! He chortled in his joy.'
explanation.definitionFit: To laugh gleefully, a word coined by Lewis Carroll beside 'frabjous' in the same verse.

clue.text: Tool for a hungry monkey

parts.note: in the fable a monkey gets a cat to pull roasting chestnuts from the fire for it

explanation.surface: An implement a starving ape might use.
explanation.walkthrough: In the fable the monkey uses the cat's foot to rake chestnuts out of the fire, hence the term for a person used as a dupe.
explanation.definitionFit: A person exploited as a dupe, from the fable of the monkey using the cat to fetch roasting chestnuts.

clue.text: One method of communication between banks

definitions.text: One method of communication between banks

parts.words: One method of communication between banks
parts.note: the banks are those of a river, and the link between them is a boat service

explanation.surface: A way that banking institutions might contact each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' suggests financial institutions; they are riverbanks, linked by a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat carrying passengers across a river connects its two shores.

clue.text: Britain's number one hero

parts.note: the song 'The British ...' praises these soldiers above every hero, and they form the First Regiment of Foot Guards

explanation.surface: Names the greatest of British heroes.
explanation.walkthrough: The march 'The British Grenadiers' sets them above Hercules and Alexander, and their regiment is the First Regiment of Foot Guards.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier of the Grenadier Guards, the senior Foot Guards regiment celebrated in a famous marching song.

clue.text: Perhaps a test of individual preference

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the following words may be put in another order

explanation.surface: Proposes an examination of what someone personally likes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' tells you to rearrange A TEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's liking for some things over others is their own discernment or palate.

clue.text: Yellow weed running wild in the paddock ?

definitions.meaning: a wild plant of the daisy family with yellow flowers, an old remedy for coughs
read literally, the foot of a young horse galloping about a field

explanation.surface: A yellow weed spreading unchecked across a horse's field.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the plant's name into the hoof of a young male horse, which is what runs about a paddock.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant is a common yellow-flowered weed; split up, the name is the hoof of a young stallion.

clue.text: Botanical sources of music

parts.note: plants of the marsh supply the vibrating tongues in oboes, clarinets and bassoons, and pan pipes were cut from them

explanation.surface: A plain description of plants that give us music.
explanation.definitionFit: Woodwind players blow through thin cane strips, and early pipes were made from marsh grasses.

clue.text: This meat is not for the carnivore

definitions.text: This meat is not for the carnivore

parts.words: This meat is not for the carnivore
parts.note: the word before 'meat' makes a confection, a candied treat rather than flesh

explanation.surface: A warning that a certain kind of meat will not please a meat-eater.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the answer before 'meat' and you get a sweetmeat, a sugary morsel that holds no flesh at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetmeat is a candy or confection, so it is no food for a flesh-eater.

clue.text: Unsuitable refreshment at a Temperance Meeting ?

definitions.text: Unsuitable refreshment at a Temperance Meeting ?

parts.words: Unsuitable refreshment at a Temperance Meeting ?
parts.note: a dessert soaked in sherry or wine would offend a gathering sworn against alcohol

explanation.surface: Someone has served the wrong food at an anti-drink gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: A tipsy cake is a British trifle-like pudding of sponge soaked in sherry or wine, so it would be out of place among teetotallers.
explanation.definitionFit: The pudding is sponge drenched in alcohol, so its name says it is drunk.

clue.text: He wants a good hiding

parts.note: a 'good hiding' sounds like a beating, but here it means a place to stay out of sight

explanation.surface: A naughty boy who seems to be asking for a thrashing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a good hiding' usually means a beating; here it means being well hidden from the world.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit withdraws from society and wants to stay out of view.

clue.text: A small measure of banter giving one the bird

parts.note: chaff is light teasing talk
an inch is a small unit of length

explanation.surface: A bit of teasing that makes someone get booed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giving one the bird' sounds like being jeered at; here 'the bird' is the definition, a small finch.
explanation.definitionFit: A common European finch with a pink breast.

clue.text: It sounds a very large' part of London

indicators.note: says the next words give a word heard aloud rather than spelt

parts.note: whopping means very large

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a district of London has an impressive-sounding size.
explanation.walkthrough: Wapping is a riverside district in east London; said aloud it matches 'whopping'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wapping is a district on the Thames in east London.

clue.text: Venomous type puts on the blurb

definitions.text: Venomous type puts on the blurb

parts.words: Venomous type puts on the blurb
parts.note: split, the name is one who adds a puff, a piece of promotional praise, to a book

explanation.surface: A spiteful writer composes the publicity on a dust jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'puff' is promotional praise, so a 'puff-adder' is one who adds the blurb; the real creature is a venomous African snake.
explanation.definitionFit: A highly venomous African viper that puffs itself up when threatened.

clue.text: But mob-caps would hardly suit them

definitions.text: But mob-caps would hardly suit them

parts.words: But mob-caps would hardly suit them
parts.note: a mob-cap is an old woman's bonnet, while the clue's 'mob' points to criminal gangs whose members wear trilbies

explanation.surface: A remark that frilly old-fashioned bonnets would not flatter certain people.
explanation.walkthrough: A mob-cap is an 18th-century woman's indoor bonnet; 'mob' also means a criminal gang, whose members would look odd in one.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a criminal mob are hoodlums and racketeers.

clue.text: He's not necessarily addicted to gin in his work

definitions.text: He's not necessarily addicted to gin in his work

parts.words: He's not necessarily addicted to gin in his work
parts.note: a gin is also a snare for animals, so this man uses gins professionally without drinking them

explanation.surface: A worker whose job seems to involve a lot of gin, though he may be sober.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin' is not the spirit: it is an old word for a snare, the tool of a man who catches animals for fur.
explanation.definitionFit: A fur hunter sets snares, which are also called gins.

clue.text: Liqueur at a fair, perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the words before it might form another word

explanation.surface: A drink sampled at a fairground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells you to rearrange AT A FAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: An almond-flavoured cordial, also the name of a small almond biscuit.

clue.text: Orange-yellow, for fans perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the words before it are only one possible arrangement

explanation.surface: Suggests a team colour that supporters might wear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells you to rearrange FOR FANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Saffron is the deep yellow-orange of the crocus spice.

clue.text: It's divine having to stand and deliver them

definitions.text: It's divine having to stand and deliver them

parts.words: It's divine having to stand and deliver them
parts.note: 'divine' is a noun for a clergyman, and 'stand and deliver' is the highwayman's demand, here meaning to stand in the pulpit and preach

explanation.surface: A lovely thing it is to be held up by a highwayman.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'divine' is a clergyman, and 'stand and deliver', the highwayman's call, here means standing up to give addresses from the pulpit.
explanation.definitionFit: Addresses from the pulpit are what a clergyman stands up to give.

clue.text: Emendator not paying his debts ?

parts.note: split as ..., the word suggests one who removes faults, an emendator, while its real sense is a debtor who fails to pay

explanation.surface: Asks whether a corrector of texts is someone who will not settle up.
explanation.walkthrough: An emendator corrects faults; reading the answer as 'de-faulter' gives exactly that, while the true sense is one who fails to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: One who fails to meet a payment due is in default on the debt.

clue.text: The one under the doctor-but not through overwork '

definitions.text: The one under the doctor-but not through overwork '

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece beneath sits after the other one

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone receiving medical care, though not because of hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under' places ONE below DR in the down entry. 'Under the doctor' also means being treated for illness, and the male bee is idle, so it never falls ill from overwork.
explanation.definitionFit: The male bee does no work in the hive, so it is an idler.

clue.text: They employ strange ruses

definitions.note: plural people who employ things, matching a plural noun

indicators.note: signals that the following letters are oddly arranged

explanation.surface: People who resort to odd tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' tells you to rearrange RUSES.
explanation.definitionFit: People who make use of something are its consumers or employers.

clue.text: Heavenly hold-up man

parts.note: a hold-up man sounds like a robber, but this figure holds up the heavens

explanation.surface: A robber with a celestial touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hold-up man' suggests a robber; the Titan of Greek myth was condemned to hold up the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titan was made to bear the heavens on his shoulders.

clue.text: It's granted by letter

parts.note: a 'letter' here is one who lets property, a landlord, not a written message

explanation.surface: Something given in writing by post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' looks like a written message; it is one who lets, a landlord, who grants a tenancy contract.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord grants a tenant a contract for occupying property for a term.

clue.text: A beastly light-weight

parts.note: the word is both a small unit of weight and the snow leopard, a wild animal

explanation.surface: An unpleasant person of little importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beastly' means 'belonging to the animal kingdom', not nasty: the snow leopard shares its name with a small unit of weight.
explanation.definitionFit: It names both a sixteenth of a pound and the snow leopard of Central Asia.

clue.text: Opened after Madame de Pompadour ?

parts.note: Madame de Pompadour is credited with saying 'after us, the deluge', so what opens after her releases a flood

explanation.surface: Asks what was unlocked after the French king's mistress had gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame de Pompadour, mistress of Louis XV, is said to have remarked 'Après nous, le déluge', so after her comes a deluge, let in by a sluice.
explanation.definitionFit: A sluice barrier holds back water, and opening it lets the deluge through.

clue.text: Diana's fans

parts.note: in the Acts of the Apostles a crowd chants 'Great is Diana' of their city, whose temple was hers

explanation.surface: Admirers of a woman named Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: In Acts 19 the people of Ephesus, whose great temple was to Diana (Artemis), shout 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians!'
explanation.definitionFit: The citizens of that Greek city in Asia Minor were devoted worshippers of the goddess Diana.

clue.text: Not the dances for those going steady " ?

definitions.text: Not the dances for those going steady " ?

parts.words: Not the dances for those going steady " ?
parts.note: the word is both a set of lively Scottish dances and a verb for staggering, which is no way to walk steadily

explanation.surface: Suggests some dances are unsuitable for a courting couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going steady' suggests a romance; here it means walking without lurching, and the answer also means staggers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means lively folk dances and also lurches, the opposite of a steady walk.
